title: Inquest into death of Casselman woman reveals complexities of Ontario's 911 system
article: The 911 call taker who was the last person to hear Kathryn Missen's voice wiped away tears and fought to compose himself as he apologized to the Casselman woman's family at a coroner's inquest Monday.

"I've never had a job like this before," Paul Sanders testified as he looked directly at Missen's three sisters and daughter, seated in the front row at the crowded inquest. "I love this job. I never want this to happen to anyone ever again. If I can make it better for future call takers, I will. You have my word."

Sanders was the first witness at the Ottawa portion of the inquest, which began last week in Sudbury and is looking into failures in Ontario's 911 system in Missen's 2014 death and a July 2013 boating accident in Sudbury that killed three people.

Sanders, 47, was a team leader at the OPP's Central Emergency Reporting Bureau in North Bay when Missen called 911 while suffering from an asthma attack. The brief recording was played for the inquest, after Missen's family was allowed to leave the room. The call lasted barely a minute.
"911. Do you require police, fire or ambulance?" Sanders says.
Missen's response is barely audible as she gasps and struggles to breathe.
"Do you need the police? Hello?" Sanders asks, before following protocol, he transfers the call to a secondary OPP call taker based in Smiths Falls, which dispatches the OPP in Eastern Ontario.
"There's a female on the line," Sanders told the new call taker. "She's still on the line. I'm not sure what she needs. She hasn't said anything."

There were further delays after that secondary call, coroner's counsel Prabhu Rajan explained to the inquest, and when an OPP officer was finally dispatched to check on Missen's address more than 90 minutes later, he never actually went to the scene. (The officer later pleaded guilty to neglect of duty, saying he'd forgotten about the call during a busy shift.)
Missen's body was found two days later by neighbours worried that they hadn't seen her. She was 54.

The inquest, with Dr. David Cameron as presiding coroner, is expected to cast a light on Ontario's complex 911 dispatch system, in which an emergency call can bounce several times around the province while it's routed to the appropriate first responder. The five-person jury cannot assign blame but will instead try to determine the circumstances of the deaths of Missen and the three Sudbury boaters and may make recommendations to prevent future deaths.
Blame is not what the Missen family is seeking.

"It was very difficult to hear Mr. Sanders' testimony, very emotional," sister Brenda Missen told reporters outside the hearing room. "We wanted him to know that we weren't holding him responsible, personally, for what happened."

Another sister, Lynne Missen Jolly, began the day's hearing with a vivid portrait of Kathryn's life - how she studied Greek and Latin in high school, her love of choral singing and her devotion to her church, St. Barnabas in the Glebe, and her interest and knowledge in herbal medicine.

Kathryn Missen was born with severe and wide-ranging food allergies and had suffered severe allergy-induced asthma attacks. She needed hospital treatment numerous times, but Sept. 1, 2014 was the first time she had ever had to call 911.
The family has been doing their own research into the circumstances of her death and was shocked to learn how 911 calls cascade through to different call takers before anyone is sent to respond.

"To me, it seems completely crazy," Kathryn's daughter, Harriet Clunie, told reporters. "It just seems a bit too complicated for something that needs to be dealt with so quickly. There are too many opportunities for human error or technical error."

An end to that two-tiered response is the first request the Missen family made in its presentation to the inquest. It also wants a method for call takers to respond to "silent calls" to 911, which might come from someone in medical distress or someone who is being threatened and too scared to speak to the call taker. The Missens also want better transparency about 911 problems and independent reviews of problems so that the OPP isn't investigating its own role in the 911 system.
The Ottawa portion of the inquest is expected to continue until Nov. 2.
